entities.name: PMID:25091082
observations: 2014 cross-sectional mailed survey of 246 practising Australian dentists; adjusted response rate was 40.1%.
Only 3.7% reported using a published dental-anxiety scale; approximately half directly asked patients about dental anxiety.
Dentists estimated high dental anxiety in 23.3% of children and 19.4% of adults seen; lack of awareness was the commonest reason for not using a published scale (56.5%).
About one-third reported undergraduate dental-anxiety training; 41.7% rated it good or better, and almost 37% expressed interest in future training.

entities.name: PMID:1829734
observations: 1991 survey of 267 Victorian dentists examined management strategies for anxious children or children with behaviour problems, not formal anxiety screening.
The available abstract does not report a named anxiety instrument, quantitative screening prevalence, or dentists' education and training needs.

entities.name: Australian screening gap
observations: In the 2014 survey, formal published-scale screening was uncommon (3.7%), whereas approximately half of dentists directly asked patients about dental anxiety.
This supports a time-specific conclusion that informal assessment was more common than validated-scale screening among surveyed Australian dentists.

entities.name: Australian training need
observations: In 2014, only about one-third of surveyed Australian dentists reported undergraduate training related to dental anxiety; 41.7% rated that training good or better and almost 37% wanted future training.
This supports a time-specific conclusion that self-reported preparation was limited and a substantial minority reported further training interest.
